summary: Describes an enhanced form of compressed RTP for links with high delay, packet loss, and reordering. It builds on the IP/UDP/RTP header compression in RFC 2508, which copes poorly with loss on such links because context gets corrupted. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Voice and video headers are mostly the same from one packet to the next, so CRTP keeps that shared information at each end and sends only what changed. This document makes that work when packets get lost on the way: the sender repeats each change, and the receiver can check it is still in step.

questions: rtp header compression on lossy links
how does crtp handle packet loss
what is the crtp headers checksum
what is the twice algorithm in crtp
subtitle: Keeps IP, UDP and RTP header compression working on links that lose, delay and reorder packets.

tldr.problem: CRTP compresses the IP, UDP and RTP headers to 2 to 4 bytes by keeping shared state at both ends, but it assumes a reliable, short, in-order link. On a lossy or slow link, one lost packet can leave the two ends with different state, and the repair needs a full round trip.
tldr.mechanism: Enhanced CRTP repeats every context update N+1 times, adds flags that carry absolute values such as the full RTP timestamp and the IPv4 ID, and adds a 16-bit headers checksum so the receiver can tell whether it is still in step.
tldr.outcome: The decompressor stays in sync over links with packet loss, reordering and long delays. The RFC also notes that the scheme cannot be negotiated by itself: each link layer needs its own way of agreeing to use it.

facts.label: New COMPRESSED_UDP flags
facts.value: F, I, dT, dI, M, S, T, P, C

today: RFC 3545 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why CRTP Breaks on Lossy Links
sections.content:
RTP header compression, described in RFC 2508, reduces the header overhead of IP/UDP/RTP datagrams by compressing the three headers, which are compressed to 2 to 4 bytes most of the time. CRTP was designed for reliable point to point links with short delays, and it does not perform well over links with a high rate of packet loss, packet reordering and long delays.

An example of such a link is a PPP session tunnelled using an IP level tunnelling protocol such as L2TP: packets inside the tunnel are carried by an IP network and may be lost and reordered, and the longer the tunnel the longer the round trip time. Another example is an IP network that uses layer 2 technologies such as ATM and Frame Relay for the access portion of the network. Those virtual circuits do not reorder packets, but they often have a low bit rate and may span a larger physical distance than a point to point serial link, so the round trip delay between the endpoints is higher and congestion in the layer 2 network can produce a higher drop rate.

RFC 3095 defines another RTP header compression scheme, Robust Header Compression, developed with wireless links as the main target. ROHC was designed with the same link assumptions as CRTP, so it also does not have to tolerate misordering of compressed packets between the compressor and the decompressor, which may occur when packets are carried in an IP tunnel across multiple hops. The authors expect enhanced CRTP to be the preferred choice where CRTP is already implemented, because the extra work is small, and in some cases the implementation simplicity of enhanced CRTP matters more than the performance advantages of ROHC.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression here works by assuming each packet's headers differ from the last in a predictable way. That assumption breaks on a tunnel or a virtual circuit where packets go missing or arrive out of order.

sections.title: The Context and How It Gets Corrupted
sections.content:
During compression of an RTP stream, a session context is defined. For each context, the session state is established and shared between the compressor and the decompressor, and compressed packets may be sent once that state is in place. The context state consists of the full IP/UDP/RTP headers, a few first order differential values, a link sequence number, a generation number and a delta encoding table.

The headers part of the context is set by the FULL_HEADER packet, which always starts a compression session. The first order differential values, or delta values, are set by sending COMPRESSED_RTP packets that include updates to them.

The context state must be synchronized between compressor and decompressor for successful decompression to take place. If the context gets out of sync, the decompressor cannot restore the compressed headers accurately. It invalidates the context and sends a CONTEXT_STATE packet to the compressor to say the context has been corrupted, and the compressor must re-establish the context. During the time the context is corrupted the decompressor discards all packets received for that context. Because context repair involves feedback from the decompressor, it takes at least as much time as the round trip time of the link, so on a link with a long round trip time and high bandwidth many packets are discarded before the context is repaired.

As long as the fields in the combined headers change as expected for the sequence of packets in a session, the decompressor can restore them from the context state. When they do not, some full or delta values must be updated. For example, the RTP timestamp is expected to increment by the delta RTP timestamp dT. If silence suppression is used, no packets are sent during silence, so when voice activity resumes the timestamp jumps by a large value instead of by dT, and an update must be sent.

If a packet that includes an update is lost, the state at the decompressor is not updated and the shared state differs at the two ends. The next packet then arrives at a decompressor whose context no longer matches the compressor's, so it cannot restore the headers accurately.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends keep a copy of the headers and of the rules for changing them. If the packet that carried a rule change is lost, the two copies differ and the receiver can no longer rebuild the headers.

sections.title: How to Prevent Context Corruption
sections.content:
The decompressor fails not when a packet is lost, but when the next compressed packet arrives. If that next packet happens to include the same context update as the lost packet, the context at the decompressor may be updated successfully and decompression may continue uninterrupted.

If the lost packet included an update to a delta field such as the delta RTP timestamp, the next packet cannot compensate for the loss, because the update of a delta value is relative to the previous packet, which was lost. But if the update is for an absolute value such as the full RTP timestamp or the RTP payload type, that update can be repeated in the next packet independently of the lost packet.

Enhanced CRTP therefore adds the ability to update the absolute values of the context selectively, rather than sending a whole FULL_HEADER packet, in addition to the existing updates of the delta values. The intent is to minimize context invalidation and so improve performance over lossy links with a long round trip time.
sections.plainLanguage: A change that is relative to the last packet cannot be recovered if that packet is lost. A change that states an absolute value can be sent again, so the receiver catches up on the next packet it does receive.

sections.title: The Extended COMPRESSED_UDP Packet
sections.content:
Some packet loss can be accommodated with the twice algorithm of RFC 2508, so long as the context stays in sync. In that algorithm the delta values are added to the previous context twice, or more, to effect the change that would have occurred if the missing packets had arrived, and the result is verified with the UDP checksum. Keeping the context in sync requires reliably communicating both the absolute value and the delta value whenever the delta value changes, and for many environments that reliability is achieved by repeating the update with each of several successive packets.

The COMPRESSED_UDP packet in RFC 2508 satisfies the need to communicate absolute values, but it is specified to reset the delta RTP timestamp. This document changes that: the T bit MAY be nonzero to indicate that the delta RTP timestamp is included explicitly rather than being reset to zero.

A second change adds another byte of flag bits to the COMPRESSED_UDP packet, so that only selected individual uncompressed fields of the RTP header are included rather than the whole RTP header being carried as part of the UDP data. The original S, T and I bits, which indicated the inclusion of deltas, are renamed dS, dT and dI, and the inclusion of absolute values is indicated by S, T and I. The M bit is absolute as before. A new flag P indicates inclusion of the absolute RTP payload type, and a new flag C indicates inclusion of the CSRC count; when C is 1, an additional byte is added after the two flag bytes carrying the absolute value of the four-bit CC field.

The third change deals with the IPv4 ID field. RFC 2508 can convey a new delta IPv4 ID in a COMPRESSED_UDP packet, but not the absolute value, which only the FULL_HEADER packet conveys. A new flag I therefore indicates inclusion of the absolute IPv4 ID value. The I flag replaces the dS flag, which is not needed in the COMPRESSED_UDP packet because the delta RTP sequence number always remains 1 in the decompressor context. IPv6 has no IP ID field, so when compressing IPv6 packets both the I and the dI flags are always 0.

The flags and sequence byte is now F | I | dT | dI | link sequence, and when F is 1 an extension flags byte M | S | T | P | C | 0 | 0 | 0 follows. When F is 0, only dI, dT and I are available and the packet includes the full RTP header; if dI is 0 the decompressor does not change deltaI, and if dT is 0 the decompressor sets deltaT to 0. When F is 1 the packet does not include the full RTP header but the selected fields; if dT is 0 the decompressor keeps the current deltaT in the context instead of setting it to 0. The bits marked 0 in the second flag byte and the CC byte SHOULD be set to zero by the sender and SHOULD be ignored by the receiver.

For usage, the compressor may periodically refresh the decompressor state using F=0 with I=1, dI=1 and dT=1, which refreshes all the context parameters. Where the delta values change frequently on a lossy link with a long round trip delay, the compressor MAY choose always to send absolute values and never delta values, using COMPRESSED_UDP packets with F=1 and any of S, T and I as necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The new packet carries a row of flag bits, one for each header field that may be sent in full. The sender sets a flag when it includes that field, so the receiver knows exactly what it is being told.

sections.title: The Headers Checksum
sections.content:
RFC 2508 describes how the UDP checksum may be used to validate header reconstruction periodically or when the twice algorithm is used. When a UDP checksum is not present, with value zero, in a stream, that validation is not possible. To cover that case, enhanced CRTP gives the compressor the option of replacing the null UDP checksum with a 16-bit headers checksum, HDRCKSUM, which the decompressor removes after validation. This option is never used with IPv6, since a null UDP checksum is not allowed there.

A new flag C in the FULL_HEADER packet indicates, when set, that all COMPRESSED_UDP and COMPRESSED_RTP packets sent in that context will have HDRCKSUM inserted. The compressor MAY set the C flag when the UDP packet carried in the FULL_HEADER packet originally contained a checksum value of zero. If the C flag is set, the FULL_HEADER packet itself MUST also have the HDRCKSUM inserted. If a packet in the same stream subsequently arrives at the compressor with a UDP checksum present, a new FULL_HEADER packet MUST be sent with the flag cleared to re-establish the context.

The HDRCKSUM is calculated in the same way as a UDP checksum except that it does not cover all of the UDP data. It is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of the pseudo-IP header, the UDP header, the first 12 bytes of the UDP data, which are assumed to hold the fixed part of an RTP header, and the CSRC list. The extended part of the RTP header beyond the CSRC list and the RTP data are not included. The HDRCKSUM is placed in the COMPRESSED_UDP or COMPRESSED_RTP packet where a UDP checksum would have been, and the decompressor MUST zero out the UDP checksum field in the reconstructed packets. For a non-RTP context there may be fewer than 12 UDP data bytes present; the HDRCKSUM is then calculated over the pseudo-IP header, the UDP header and the data bytes that are present, and if the number of data bytes is odd a zero padding byte is appended for the calculation but not transmitted.

The HDRCKSUM does not validate the RTP data. If the link layer delivers packets without checking for errors, errors in the RTP data will not be detected. Over such links the compressor SHOULD add the HDRCKSUM if a UDP checksum is not present, and the decompressor SHOULD validate each reconstructed packet to make sure at least the headers are correct, so the packet is delivered to the right destination.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver recomputes the checksum over the headers it rebuilt and compares it with the one the sender put in. If they differ, the two ends have drifted apart and the receiver knows it.

sections.title: Achieving Robust Operation
sections.content:
Enhanced CRTP achieves robust operation by sending changes multiple times to keep the compressor and decompressor in sync. This method is characterized by a number N that represents the quality of the link between the hosts: it means that the probability of more than N adjacent packets getting lost on the link is small. For every change in a full value or a delta value, if the compressor includes the change in N+1 consecutive packets, the decompressor can keep its context in sync using the twice algorithm so long as no more than N adjacent packets are lost.

The link sequence number cycles in 16 packets, so it is not always clear how many packets were lost. If the previous link sequence number was 5 and the current number is 4, one possibility is that 15 packets were lost, and another is that packet 5 arrived before packet 4 and they are really adjacent. If there is an interpretation of the sequence numbers that could be a gap of less than N+1, the twice algorithm may be applied that many times and verified with the UDP checksum or the HDRCKSUM.

When more than N packets are lost, all of the repetitions of an update might have been lost, and the decompressor can still try to recover by guessing how many packets were lost and applying the twice algorithm that many times. However, since the IPv4 ID field is not included in the checksum, this does not validate the IPv4 ID. The conclusion is that for IPv4, if more than N packets were lost, the decompressor SHOULD NOT try to recover using the twice algorithm and instead SHOULD invalidate the context and send a CONTEXT_STATE packet. In IPv6 the decompressor MAY always try to recover from packet loss by using the twice algorithm and verifying the result with the UDP checksum.

It is up to the implementation to derive an appropriate N for a link. The value is maintained independently for each context. When compressing a new stream, the compressor sets a value of N for that context and sends N+1 FULL_HEADER packets, and it MUST repeat each subsequent COMPRESSED_UDP update N+1 times. The value of N may be changed for an existing context by sending a new sequence of FULL_HEADER packets.

The decompressor learns the value of N by counting how many times the FULL_HEADER packet is repeated and storing the result in the corresponding context. If some of the FULL_HEADER packets are lost, the decompressor may still determine the correct value of N by observing the change in the 4-bit sequence number carried in them. Any inaccuracy in the counting leads the decompressor to assume a smaller N than the compressor is sending, which is safe, because the only negative consequence is that the decompressor might send a CONTEXT_STATE packet when it was not really necessary.

Sending FULL_HEADER packets is also triggered by a change in one of the fields held constant in the context, such as the IP TOS. If such a change occurs while the compressor is in the middle of sending the N+1 FULL_HEADER packets, the compressor MUST send N+1 FULL_HEADER packets after making the change. That could leave the decompressor receiving more than N+1 FULL_HEADER packets in a row, so it would assume a larger value for N than is correct, which could lead to an undetected loss of context synchronization. The compressor MUST therefore change the generation number in the context and in the FULL_HEADER packet when it begins sending the sequence of N+1 FULL_HEADER packets, so the decompressor can detect the new sequence. For IPv4 this is a change in behaviour relative to RFC 2508.

CONTEXT_STATE packets SHOULD also be repeated N+1 times, using the same sequence number for each context, to give a similar measure of robustness against packet loss. Here N can be the largest N of all contexts included in the CONTEXT_STATE packet, or any number the decompressor finds necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Choose a number N that reflects how bad the link is, then send every change N+1 times. If at most N packets in a row are lost, at least one copy of the change gets through and the two ends stay in step.

sections.title: Agreeing to Use Enhanced CRTP
sections.content:
The use of IP/UDP/RTP compression over a particular link is a function of the link-layer protocol, and it is expected that negotiation of the use of CRTP will be defined separately for each link layer.

For link layers that already have a negotiation for the use of CRTP as specified in RFC 2508, an extension to that negotiation will be required to indicate use of the enhanced CRTP defined in this document, since the syntax of the existing packet formats has been extended.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here decides how two ends agree to use the scheme. Each link type has to say so in its own way, because the packet formats changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because encryption eliminates the redundancy that this compression scheme tries to exploit, there is some inducement to forego encryption in order to achieve operation over a low-bandwidth link. However, for cases where encryption of data and not headers is satisfactory, RTP does specify an alternative encryption method in which only the RTP payload is encrypted and the headers are left in the clear, which allows compression to still be applied.

A malfunctioning or malicious compressor could cause the decompressor to reconstitute packets that do not match the original packets but still have valid IP, UDP and RTP headers and possibly even valid UDP checksums. Such corruption may be detected with end-to-end authentication and integrity mechanisms, which are not affected by the compression; constant portions of authentication headers will be compressed as described in RFC 2507.

No authentication is performed on the CONTEXT_STATE control packet sent by this protocol. An attacker with access to the link between the decompressor and compressor could inject false CONTEXT_STATE packets and cause compression efficiency to be reduced, probably resulting in congestion on the link, although an attacker with access to the link could also disrupt the traffic in many other ways.

A potential denial-of-service threat exists when using compression techniques that have a non-uniform receiver-end computational load: an attacker can inject pathological datagrams into the stream which are complex to decompress and overload the receiver. This compression does not exhibit any significant non-uniformity.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressing and encrypting fight each other, because encryption removes the repetition that compression relies on. Encrypting only the payload and leaving the headers readable keeps both working.

viz.caption: THE NEW FLAGS BYTES OF AN ENHANCED COMPRESSED_UDP PACKET

data.title: Flags and sequence byte, extension flags byte, CC byte

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Set when the extension flags byte is present.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Absolute RTP sequence number is included.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: Absolute RTP payload type is included.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: CC
fields.desc: Count of CSRC identifiers in the lower 4 bits. This byte is present when C is 1.

items.title: Delta update
items.text: A change relative to the previous packet. If that packet is lost, the change cannot be recovered.

items.title: Absolute update
items.text: A full value, such as the RTP timestamp or the IPv4 ID. It can be repeated in the next packet.

items.title: Repeat N+1 times
items.text: Every change is sent N+1 consecutive times, where N describes the link.

items.title: Check with HDRCKSUM
items.text: A 16-bit checksum over the rebuilt headers tells the receiver whether it is still in step.
